Personally I see rocket first stages as being something that's more useful to military projects than commercial ones. The early days of space exploration were driven by the need to get weapons to an enemy as quickly as possible. Even NASA's purely civilian projects essentially amounted to "look what we can do, don't fuck with us."

For the future of affordible space exploration my money would be on rockoons. A balloon first stage gets you out of the troposphere almost for free, so that by the time you're firing a rocket there's already almost no air resistance. Meaning the rockets can be cheaper and the vehicles don't have to be aerodynamic.

Reentry is another one. The military couldn't afford to have a capsule end up in the soviet union or china, so they aerobraked them out of orbit in one or (max) two reentry events, requiring extremely heavy heat shields and capsule insulation. I'd argue it was also test run for their MIRV program. A much more efficient way to do it would be to do multiple skips, gradually bleeding velocity and dispersing the heat over several hours, before a final, gentle reentry in a lightweight vehicle.

I'd argue for massive single stage vehicles with collapsible fuselages. As you exit the atmosphere, you simply don't need cabin space for anything more than a seat per person plus headroom to float past the seats. What you do need is a shitton of fuel. If the fuel tank crushes like a water bottle, you can have full suites fold out to take up it's volume as fuel is depleted. Much larger ships built for continuous space travel rather than planetary ferrying could use the former fuel volume for a drydock to build more ships.
